issue_context.title: systemctl timestamp formats inadequate for machine parsing, no epoch
issue_context.body:
**systemd version the issue has been seen with**
systemd 250

**Expected behaviour you didn't see**
None of the timestamp formats available in `systemctl` are machine parseable. For instance, GNU date has issues with all of those.
The `--timestamp` parameter inconveniently accepts only arbitrary human readable values.

**Steps to reproduce the problem**
`# LANG=C systemctl show systemd-journald | grep Timestamp`
no epoch values here

```
# systemctl --help
...
                         'pretty' (default): 'Day YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS TZ
                         'us': 'Day YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.UUUUUU TZ
                         'utc': 'Day YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS UTC
                         'us+utc': 'Day YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.UUUUUU UT
```

The epoch provides a convenient time specification for machine parsing. Sadly, systemctl isn't doing much in the way of enabling its output to be parsable by scripts easily.

Seeing as there is a choice of format, one would expect epoch there. For some reason, it's either 'us' or 'utc' or combination of both. Shouldn't there be a greater choice of formats here?

I don't see much difference between these formats anyway. None of them is accepted by `date` for machine parsing:

```
# date -d$(systemctl show --timestamp=pretty systemd-journald -P ActiveEnterTimestamp)
date: extra operand ‘19:20:05’
Try 'date --help' for more information.
# date -d$(systemctl show --timestamp=utc systemd-journald -P ActiveEnterTimestamp)
date: extra operand ‘19:20:05’
Try 'date --help' for more information.
# date -d$(systemctl show --timestamp=us+utc systemd-journald -P ActiveEnterTimestamp)
date: extra operand ‘19:20:05’
Try 'date --help' for more information.
# date -d$(systemctl show --timestamp=us systemd-journald -P ActiveEnterTimestamp)
date: extra operand ‘19:20:05’
Try 'date --help' for more information.
```

Please allow at least epoch to be displayed, or at best a free format string, with sequences similar to FORMAT used by `GNU Coreutils` (`%s` = epoch, etc).
comments:
> I don't see much difference between these formats anyway. None of them is accepted by `date` for machine parsing:
> 
> ```
> # date -d$(systemctl show --timestamp=pretty systemd-journald -P ActiveEnterTimestamp)
> date: extra operand ‘19:20:05’
> Try 'date --help' for more information.
> # date -d$(systemctl show --timestamp=utc systemd-journald -P ActiveEnterTimestamp)
> date: extra operand ‘19:20:05’
> Try 'date --help' for more information.
> # date -d$(systemctl show --timestamp=us+utc systemd-journald -P ActiveEnterTimestamp)
> date: extra operand ‘19:20:05’
> Try 'date --help' for more information.
> # date -d$(systemctl show --timestamp=us systemd-journald -P ActiveEnterTimestamp)
> date: extra operand ‘19:20:05’
> Try 'date --help' for more information.
> ```

This part isn't true - you have to quote the timestamp string, as it contains spaces:
```
$ date -d "$(systemctl show systemd-journald -P ActiveEnterTimestamp)"
Sat Dec 11 03:25:57 PM CET 2021
```

(`date` is even telling you that you have extra arguments on the command line)

Well spotted, that is precisely why the epoch format is needed. You avoid the need to run it past `date` to begin with.
The epoch requires no quoting to be useful for anything and is independent of any political timezone slant.

did you see systemd.time(7) man page? The format we generate is certainly machine parseable, because it's the format we parse all the time, for example in `journalctl --after=…` and similar.

Use `systemd-analyze timestamp …` for a tool that will parse/validate timestamps in the documented format.

what do you mean by "epoch format"? seconds since 1970?

so given we thoroughly established that all our formats are machine parsable by GNU date and by systemd, and that out format is pretty well documented, and we even provide you with parsing/validation/normalization tool set, can we close this?

(I mean, I'd not be opposed to adding a new value to `--timestamp=` that permits requesting seconds since 1970 output. After all, when parsing we actually accept that already, see man page, by prefixing with '@')

Of course I've gone through all that effort.

It's beside the point what format is used within systemd, that's not what this issue is about. These formats are poorly suited for machine parsing without passing through other tools. So is `systemd-analyse timestamp`, it's more of a command for internal uses.

If this bug is closed, the command's output will still remain inadequate for straight machine parsing. At the end of the day, why have 'us' or 'utc' or 'pretty', all of which are pretty much similar, and no epoch?

Epoch time is a nice way of interoperating with other commands. No overhead is necessary to make use of timestamps elsewhere. `date` was an example.

To give the choice of a timestamp only within the bounds of the formats used internally in systemd is odd.

This may help:

```bash
systemctl show -p ActiveEnterTimestamp service1 | sed -e 's/^ActiveEnterTimestamp=//' | awk '{ printf("%s %s", $2, $3) }' | xargs -I %% date --date="%%" '+%s'
```

Result: `1669127394`

You don't need the `sed` or the `awk` though:

```
date --date="$(systemctl show --value -p ActiveEnterTimestamp service1)" '+%s'
```

review_comments: i think this should be moved 6 lines up, i.e. before the > 9999 thing. Because the the check it does doesn't apply to TIMESTAMP_UNIX at all: we can output anything we can store in usec_t pretty much.

hmm, so here you convert microseconds since 1970 to "broken down" (i.e. calendar) time first, via `localtime_or_gmtime()` and then convert it back to seconds since 1970 via `strftime()`'s `%s` specifier. Please just use the value as is, i.e. add right after the timestamp-is-unset check above just:

```c
r = snprintf(buf, l, "@" FMT_USEC, t / USEC_PER_SEC);  /* round down µs → s */
if (r < 0 || (size_t) r >= l)        
        return NULL;
```

That way we don't have do the roundtripping through the calendar time. Which should make things a bit more robust, if between the forth and back conversion the timezone or summer time changes or so.
